math.title: Five brutal exam equations
math.context: Decide whether each claim is true or false. Five different equations; do not reuse roots across letters.
statements: The system $\sqrt{2x+3}=y$, $y=x-1$, $y\ge 0$ has exactly two real solutions $(x,y)$.
After clearing denominators, $\dfrac{x+1}{x-2}+\dfrac{x-2}{x+1}=\dfrac{5}{2}$ has exactly two domain-legal real roots, both different from $\pm 1$ and $2$.
The equation $|x^{2}-5x+6|=x-2$ has a real solution strictly larger than $4$.
There exists a real parameter $k$ such that $x^{2}-2kx+(k^{2}-1)=0$ has a double root at $x=0$.
$\log_{3}(x-1)+\log_{3}(x+1)=\log_{3}(2x+1)$ forces $x=1$ as its only candidate, but $x=1$ is outside the log domain, so the equation has no real solution.
math.solution_overview: Five independent equation traps. The radical system $\sqrt{2x+3}=x-1$ with $x\ge 1$ squares to $x^{2}-4x-2=0$; only $x=2+\sqrt{6}$ survives the domain, so there is one solution pair, not two. The rational equation clears to $(x-5)(x+4)=0$ with both roots legal. The absolute equation $|x^{2}-5x+6|=x-2$ forces $x\ge 2$ and admits only $x=2$ and $x=4$. A double root at $0$ for $x^{2}-2kx+(k^{2}-1)$ would need $k=0$ and $k^{2}-1=0$ at once — impossible. The log equation has domain $x>1$ and the genuine root $x=1+\sqrt{3}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Substitute $y=x-1$ into the radical equation and enforce $y\ge 0$, i.e. $x\ge 1$:
$$
\sqrt{2x+3}=x-1.
$$

Square both sides (valid once the right-hand side is nonnegative):
$$
2x+3=(x-1)^{2}=x^{2}-2x+1.
$$

Bring all terms to one side:
$$
0=x^{2}-2x+1-2x-3=x^{2}-4x-2.
$$

The quadratic formula gives
$$
x=\frac{4\pm\sqrt{16+8}}{2}=\frac{4\pm\sqrt{24}}{2}=\frac{4\pm 2\sqrt{6}}{2}=2\pm\sqrt{6}.
$$

Only $x=2+\sqrt{6}\approx 4.45$ satisfies $x\ge 1$; the companion $2-\sqrt{6}\approx -0.45$ is extraneous. The corresponding $y=(2+\sqrt{6})-1=1+\sqrt{6}$ is unique as well.

Hence there is exactly **one** real solution pair, not two. The claim is false.

Back-substitution: $y=(2+\sqrt{6})-1=1+\sqrt{6}>0$ and $\sqrt{2(2+\sqrt{6})+3}=\sqrt{7+2\sqrt{6}}=\sqrt{(\sqrt{6}+1)^{2}}=1+\sqrt{6}$, confirming the unique pair.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Domain first: $x\neq 2$ and $x\neq -1$. Clear denominators by multiplying through by $2(x-2)(x+1)$:
$$
2(x+1)^{2}+2(x-2)^{2}=5(x-2)(x+1).
$$

Expand the left-hand side:
$$
2(x^{2}+2x+1)+2(x^{2}-4x+4)=2x^{2}+4x+2+2x^{2}-8x+8=4x^{2}-4x+10.
$$

Expand the right-hand side:
$$
5(x^{2}-x-2)=5x^{2}-5x-10.
$$

Bring all terms to one side:
$$
0=5x^{2}-5x-10-4x^{2}+4x-10=x^{2}-x-20.
$$

Factor:
$$
x^{2}-x-20=(x-5)(x+4).
$$

The candidates are $x=5$ and $x=-4$. Both avoid the poles $x=\pm 1$ and $x=2$, so both are domain-legal. Exactly two legal roots — the claim is true.

Spot-check $x=5$: $(5+1)/(5-2)+(5-2)/(5+1)=6/3+3/6=2+1/2=5/2$. Spot-check $x=-4$: $(-3)/(-6)+(-6)/(-3)=1/2+2=5/2$. Both work.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The right-hand side forces the domain restriction $x-2\ge 0$, i.e. $x\ge 2$, because an absolute value cannot equal a negative number.

Factor the inside:
$$
x^{2}-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3).
$$

For $x>2$ one may divide by the positive factor $x-2$:
$$
|x-3|=1\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x-3=\pm 1.
$$

The two cases give
$$
x-3=1\Rightarrow x=4,\qquad x-3=-1\Rightarrow x=2.
$$

(The formal root $x=2$ is the boundary and should be checked separately; it works: both sides vanish, since $|(2-2)(2-3)|=0=2-2$.)

The only solutions are therefore $x=2$ and $x=4$. Neither is **strictly larger than** $4$. The claim is false.

For $x>4$ one would have $|x-3|=1$ only at $x=4$ among the candidates already found; no third root appears from either case of the absolute value.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Write $f(x)=x^{2}-2kx+(k^{2}-1)$. A double root at $x=0$ requires both
$$
f(0)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad f'(0)=0.
$$

Compute the constant term:
$$
f(0)=k^{2}-1.
$$

Differentiate:
$$
f'(x)=2x-2k,\qquad f'(0)=-2k.
$$

The derivative condition forces $k=0$. Then
$$
f(0)=0^{2}-1=-1\neq 0.
$$

The two conditions cannot hold simultaneously for any real $k$. (Equivalently: the roots are $k\pm 1$, and $k+1=k-1=0$ is impossible.) No such parameter exists; the claim is false.

Completing the square $f(x)=(x-k)^{2}-1$ shows the graph is a vertical translate of $y=x^{2}-1$; it never touches the origin with a horizontal tangent.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Domain of the log equation: $x-1>0$, $x+1>0$, and $2x+1>0$. The strongest cut is
$$
x>1.
$$

Combine the left-hand side via the product rule for logs:
$$
\log_{3}\bigl((x-1)(x+1)\bigr)=\log_{3}(2x+1).
$$

Since $\log_{3}$ is one-to-one,
$$
x^{2}-1=2x+1\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x^{2}-2x-2=0.
$$

The quadratic formula gives
$$
x=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{4+8}}{2}=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{12}}{2}=\frac{2\pm 2\sqrt{3}}{2}=1\pm\sqrt{3}.
$$

Only $x=1+\sqrt{3}\approx 2.73$ lies in the domain $x>1$. Direct substitution confirms it works. So a real solution **does** exist; the claim that the equation has none (and that $x=1$ is the only candidate) is false.

The discarded root $1-\sqrt{3}\approx -0.73$ fails $x>1$, and $x=1$ itself makes $\log_{3}(x-1)$ undefined — so $x=1$ was never a candidate.

So the statement is False.

math.title: One brutal two-unknown setup — five counterfactual traps
math.context:
A workshop sells only type-$A$ kits and type-$B$ kits. In one week it sold a total of $100$ kits and booked revenue $€\,7100$. Type $A$ sells at $€\,50$ each and type $B$ at $€\,80$ each:
$$
a+b=100,\qquad 50a+80b=7100.
$$
The unique baseline solution is the factual starting point. Decide whether each counterfactual claim is true or false.
statements: The unique baseline solution is $(a,b)=(30,70)$.
If the type-$B$ price had been $€\,90$ instead of $€\,80$, with the same count $a+b=100$ and the same revenue $€\,7100$, then $b$ would have fallen below $60$.
If management had sold $10$ fewer type-$A$ kits and $10$ more type-$B$ kits than the baseline, revenue would have risen by exactly $€\,300$.
If total kits stayed $100$ but the revenue target rose to $€\,8200$ at the same prices, no nonnegative solution $(a,b)$ would exist, because an all-$B$ week only reaches $€\,8000$.
If prices stayed $€\,50$ and $€\,80$ but the shop sold the swapped mix $(70,30)$ instead of the baseline $(30,70)$, revenue would still be $€\,7100$ because only the kit labels changed.
math.solution_overview: Solve the baseline linear system once: substitute $a=100-b$ into the revenue equation $50a+80b=7100$ to get $5000+30b=7100$, hence $b=70$ and $a=30$. Each later claim is a one-parameter counterfactual — a price change to $€\,90$ (forcing $b=52.5<60$), a quantity shift of ten kits (raising revenue by exactly $€\,300$), an unreachable revenue ceiling of $8200>8000=R_{\max}$, or a fake invariance under swapping the sales mix (which actually drops revenue to $€\,5900$). Only the swapped-mix invariance fails.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Eliminate $a$ via the count constraint:
$$
a=100-b.
$$

Substitute into the revenue equation:
$$
50(100-b)+80b=7100.
$$

Expand:
$$
5000-50b+80b=7100\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 5000+30b=7100.
$$

Isolate the $b$-term:
$$
30b=7100-5000=2100\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad b=\frac{2100}{30}=70.
$$

Then $a=100-70=30$. The coefficient matrix of the $2\times 2$ system has determinant
$$
\begin{vmatrix}1&1\\50&80\end{vmatrix}=80-50=30\neq 0,
$$
so the solution is unique. The baseline is exactly $(a,b)=(30,70)$.

Cross-check via elimination of $b$: from $a+b=100$ and $50a+80b=7100$, multiply the first by $50$ to get $50a+50b=5000$, subtract from the revenue equation to leave $30b=2100$, same result.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Keep the count constraint $a+b=100$ but replace the type-$B$ unit price by $€\,90$. The counterfactual money equation is
$$
50a+90b=7100,\qquad a=100-b.
$$

Substitute $a$:
$$
50(100-b)+90b=7100.
$$

Expand:
$$
5000-50b+90b=7100\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 5000+40b=7100.
$$

Isolate $b$:
$$
40b=2100\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad b=\frac{2100}{40}=52.5.
$$

Compare with the threshold $60$:
$$
52.5<60.
$$

Relative to the baseline $b=70$, the higher $B$-price forces fewer $B$-kits to hit the same revenue. The claim is true.

Cross-check: $a=100-52.5=47.5$ and $50\cdot 47.5+90\cdot 52.5=2375+4725=7100$, confirming the counterfactual solution.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The proposed shift replaces ten $A$-kits by ten $B$-kits:
$$
(30,70)\mapsto(20,80).
$$

Each such one-for-one replacement changes revenue by the unit price gap:
$$
80-50=30.
$$

Ten replacements therefore change revenue by
$$
10\cdot 30=300.
$$

Direct check of the new mix:
$$
50\cdot 20=1000,\qquad 80\cdot 80=6400,
$$
$$
1000+6400=7400=7100+300.
$$

Revenue rises by exactly $€\,300$. The claim is true.

Alternatively, new revenue $=50\cdot 20+80\cdot 80=1000+6400=7400$, and $7400-7100=300$ matches the ten-kit price-gap argument exactly.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

With prices $50$ and $80$ and a fixed total of $100$ kits, revenue is the convex combination
$$
R=50a+80b=50(100-b)+80b=5000+30b.
$$

Since $0\le b\le 100$, the maximum occurs at $b=100$:
$$
R_{\max}=5000+30\cdot 100=5000+3000=8000,
$$
i.e. an all-$B$ week.

The target $8200$ exceeds this ceiling:
$$
8200>8000.
$$

No nonnegative $(a,b)$ can hit it. The claim — including its “all-$B$ reaches only $8000$” reason — is true.

Solving $5000+30b=8200$ formally gives $30b=3200$, $b=3200/30\approx 106.67>100$, which lies outside the feasible kit range $[0,100]$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Evaluate revenue at the swapped mix $(70,30)$:
$$
50\cdot 70=3500,\qquad 80\cdot 30=2400,
$$
$$
3500+2400=5900.
$$

Compare with the baseline:
$$
5900\neq 7100,\qquad 7100-5900=1200.
$$

That is $1200$ euros short of the baseline $7100$. Swapping quantities changes the weighted sum because the two prices differ; “only the labels changed” is not an invariance of the linear form $50a+80b$.

The claim is false.

The linear form $50a+80b$ is symmetric in the kit counts only if the prices were equal; here $50\neq 80$, so swapping $(30,70)$ for $(70,30)$ must change revenue.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Mixed absolute, radical, rational, quadratic inequality, absolute-vs-quadratic
math.context: Decide whether each claim is true or false. The five letters deliberately mix five different equation/inequality types — absolute-value, radical, rational, quadratic inequality, and absolute-versus-quadratic — in the hard exam style.
statements: The inequality $|x+2|+|x-5|\le 9$ holds for every real $x$ in the closed interval $[-3,6]$ and for no $x$ outside that interval.
The radical equation $\sqrt{2x-1}+\sqrt{x+4}=5$ has unique real solution $x=80-10\sqrt{59}$.
After excluding poles, $\dfrac{1}{x-1}-\dfrac{1}{x+1}=\dfrac{1}{2}$ has exactly one domain-legal real root.
The rational inequality $\dfrac{(x-2)(x-3)}{x-4}\ge 0$ holds precisely on the set $[2,3]\cup(4,+\infty)$.
The mixed equation $|2x-1|=x^{2}-x-1$ has exactly two distinct real solutions.
math.solution_overview: Five hard mixed types. Absolute distances to $-2$ and $5$ sum to at most $9$ precisely on $[-3,6]$ (constant $7$ on the middle segment, linear growth outside). The radical equation $\sqrt{2x-1}+\sqrt{x+4}=5$ squares twice and keeps only $80-10\sqrt{59}$. The rational difference of unit fractions equals $1/2$ at both $\pm\sqrt{5}$ — two legal roots, not one. Sign-charting $(x-2)(x-3)/(x-4)$ yields $[2,3]\cup(4,+\infty)$. Absolute-versus-quadratic $|2x-1|=x^{2}-x-1$ retains exactly the two survivors $x=3$ and $x=-2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The expression $|x+2|+|x-5|$ is the sum of distances from $x$ to $-2$ and to $5$. The critical points are $x=-2$ and $x=5$.

On the middle interval $[-2,5]$ the sum collapses to the constant
$$
(x+2)+(5-x)=7\le 9,
$$
so the whole middle interval is allowed.

For $x>5$:
$$
(x+2)+(x-5)=2x-3\le 9\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 2x\le 12\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x\le 6.
$$

For $x<-2$:
$$
(-x-2)+(5-x)=3-2x\le 9\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad -2x\le 6\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x\ge -3.
$$

Combining the three pieces gives exactly $[-3,6]$. Outside that interval the sum exceeds $9$. The claim is true.

At the endpoints: $|-3+2|+|-3-5|=1+8=9$ and $|6+2|+|6-5|=8+1=9$, so both $-3$ and $6$ are included, matching the closed interval.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Domain: $2x-1\ge 0$ and $x+4\ge 0$, i.e. $x\ge\tfrac12$. Isolate one radical:
$$
\sqrt{2x-1}=5-\sqrt{x+4}.
$$

The right-hand side must be nonnegative, so $\sqrt{x+4}\le 5$, i.e. $x+4\le 25$, hence $x\le 21$. Squaring once:
$$
2x-1=25-10\sqrt{x+4}+(x+4)\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x-30=-10\sqrt{x+4}.
$$

Hence $30-x=10\sqrt{x+4}$ (so also $x\le 30$). Square again:
$$
(30-x)^{2}=100(x+4)\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x^{2}-60x+900=100x+400,
$$
$$
x^{2}-160x+500=0.
$$

The discriminant is $25600-2000=23600=400\cdot 59$, so
$$
x=80\pm 10\sqrt{59}.
$$

Only the smaller root $80-10\sqrt{59}\approx 3.19$ lies in $[\tfrac12,21]$ and survives back-substitution; the larger root is extraneous. Unique real solution — the claim is true.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Domain: $x\neq\pm 1$. Combine the left-hand side over a common denominator:
$$
\frac{1}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x+1}=\frac{(x+1)-(x-1)}{(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{2}{x^{2}-1}.
$$

The equation becomes
$$
\frac{2}{x^{2}-1}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Cross-multiply (or take reciprocals):
$$
x^{2}-1=4\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x^{2}=5\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x=\pm\sqrt{5}.
$$

Numerically $\sqrt{5}\approx 2.236$ and $-\sqrt{5}\approx -2.236$. Both avoid the poles $\pm 1$, so both are domain-legal.

There are **two** legal roots, not exactly one. The claim is false.

Spot-check $x=\sqrt{5}$: $2/(5-1)=2/4=1/2$. Spot-check $x=-\sqrt{5}$: $2/(5-1)=1/2$ again. Both roots are genuine.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Critical points: zeros $x=2$, $x=3$ and pole $x=4$ (excluded). Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | $(x-2)(x-3)$ | $x-4$ | quotient |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,2)$ | $+$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $(2,3)$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $(3,4)$ | $+$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $(4,+\infty)$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ |

Include the zeros $x=2$ and $x=3$ (numerator vanishes, quotient $0\ge 0$) and exclude the pole $x=4$. The solution set is exactly
$$
[2,3]\cup(4,+\infty),
$$
matching the claim.

Test points confirm the chart: at $x=0$ the quotient is $({-2})({-3})/({-4})=-6/{-4}<0$; at $x=2.5$ it is $(0.5)({-0.5})/({-1.5})>0$; at $x=5$ it is $(3)(2)/(1)>0$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The right-hand side must be nonnegative:
$$
x^{2}-x-1\ge 0\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad x\le\frac{1-\sqrt{5}}{2}\ \text{ or }\ x\ge\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}.
$$

**Positive branch.** Solve $2x-1=x^{2}-x-1$:
$$
0=x^{2}-3x\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x(x-3)=0,
$$
so $x=0$ or $x=3$. Only $x=3$ lies in the RHS-nonnegative set. Check: LHS $=|6-1|=5$ and RHS $=9-3-1=5$.

**Negative branch.** Solve $2x-1=-(x^{2}-x-1)=-x^{2}+x+1$:
$$
x^{2}+x-2=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad(x+2)(x-1)=0,
$$
so $x=-2$ or $x=1$. At $x=1$ the RHS equals $-1<0$, illegal. At $x=-2$: LHS $=|-4-1|=5$ and RHS $=4+2-1=5$.

Survivors: $x=3$ and $x=-2$. Exactly two distinct real solutions. The claim is true.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Quadratic family with a parameter — critical cases
math.context:
For each real parameter $m$, define
$$
f_m(x)=x^{2}-2mx+(m^{2}-1).
$$
Decide whether each claim about this family is true or false.
statements: For every real $m$, the equation $f_m(x)=0$ has two distinct real roots.
The vertex $y$-coordinate of $y=f_m(x)$ equals $-1$ for every $m$.
If $m=2$, then the roots are $x=1$ and $x=3$.
There exists a real $m$ for which both roots are equal to $0$.
The axis of symmetry is $x=m$, so as $m$ increases the axis moves right, and at $m=0$ the axis is the $y$-axis.
math.solution_overview: Complete the square or expand the discriminant in $m$: $\Delta=(2m)^{2}-4(m^{2}-1)=4m^{2}-4m^{2}+4=4>0$ for every real $m$, so the roots are always the distinct pair $m\pm 1$. Completing the square yields $f_m(x)=(x-m)^{2}-1$, whose axis is $x=m$ and whose vertex height is constantly $-1$. Specializing to $m=2$ gives the concrete roots $1$ and $3$. A double root at $0$ would need $m=0$ and $m^{2}-1=0$ together — impossible.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The discriminant of $f_m$ as a quadratic in $x$ is
$$
\Delta=(2m)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot(m^{2}-1).
$$

Expand term by term:
$$
4m^{2}-4m^{2}+4=4.
$$

Since $\Delta=4>0$ for every real $m$, there are always two distinct real roots. The quadratic formula gives them explicitly:
$$
x=\frac{2m\pm\sqrt{4}}{2}=\frac{2m\pm 2}{2}=m\pm 1.
$$

These differ by $2$ for every $m$, so they never coalesce. Completing the square
$$
f_m(x)=(x-m)^{2}-1
$$
shows the same: the horizontal line $y=0$ always cuts the upward parabola at two points. The claim is true.

Explicitly the two roots $m+1$ and $m-1$ are distinct because $(m+1)-(m-1)=2\neq 0$ for every real $m$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A monic quadratic $x^{2}-Sx+P$ has axis $x=S/2$. Here $S=2m$, so the axis is
$$
x=\frac{2m}{2}=m.
$$

The vertex $y$-coordinate is the value on the axis:
$$
f_m(m)=m^{2}-2m\cdot m+(m^{2}-1).
$$

Simplify step by step:
$$
m^{2}-2m^{2}+m^{2}-1=(m^{2}-2m^{2}+m^{2})-1=-1.
$$

Completing the square gives the same constant:
$$
f_m(x)=(x-m)^{2}-1,
$$
whose minimum is $-1$ for every $m$. The claim is true.

Geometrically every parabola in the family sits with its vertex exactly one unit below the $x$-axis, independent of the horizontal shift $m$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Specialize the family to the concrete parameter $m=2$:
$$
f_2(x)=x^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot x+(2^{2}-1)=x^{2}-4x+3.
$$

Factor by inspection (or by the general root formula $m\pm 1$):
$$
x^{2}-4x+3=(x-1)(x-3),
$$
because $1+3=4$ and $1\cdot 3=3$.

The roots are therefore $x=1$ and $x=3$, which matches $2\pm 1$. Direct substitution also checks:
$$
f_2(1)=1-4+3=0,\qquad f_2(3)=9-12+3=0.
$$

The claim is true.

Using $m\pm 1$ at $m=2$ recovers $2+1=3$ and $2-1=1$ instantly, matching the factored form $(x-1)(x-3)$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

If both roots equal $0$, then $f_m$ would have a double root at $0$, requiring
$$
f_m(0)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad f_m'(0)=0.
$$

Now $f_m(0)=m^{2}-1$ and $f_m'(x)=2x-2m$, so
$$
f_m'(0)=-2m=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad m=0.
$$

But then
$$
f_0(0)=0^{2}-1=-1\neq 0.
$$

Equivalently: the roots are $m\pm 1$, and requiring both to vanish gives the contradictory system
$$
m+1=0\quad\text{and}\quad m-1=0.
$$

No such $m$ exists; the claim is false.

If one tried to force a root at $0$ with multiplicity one only, $f_m(0)=m^{2}-1=0$ would need $m=\pm 1$, but then the other root is $m\mp 1\neq 0$ — still not a double root at zero.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

For the monic quadratic $x^{2}-2mx+(m^{2}-1)$, the axis of symmetry is half the linear coefficient:
$$
x=\frac{2m}{2}=m.
$$

Equivalently, completing the square yields $f_m(x)=(x-m)^{2}-1$, whose axis is visibly $x=m$.

As the parameter $m$ increases, this vertical line translates to the right at unit speed: if $m$ rises by $1$, the axis moves from $x=m$ to $x=m+1$.

Setting $m=0$ places the axis at
$$
x=0,
$$
i.e. on the $y$-axis.

All three clauses of the claim hold.

Differentiating the completed-square form also shows $f_m'(x)=2(x-m)$, which vanishes only on the axis $x=m$, confirming the symmetry line.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Courier tariff — affine day/night word problem
math.context: A courier charges a daytime base fee of $€\,12$ plus $€\,0.8$ per kilometre. Night runs use the same kilometre rate but add a flat night surcharge of $€\,5$. Let $d>0$ be the distance in kilometres. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: The daytime bill for distance $d$ is exactly $12+0.8d$ euros.
If the same distance were run at night, the night bill would be exactly $€\,5$ more than the daytime bill for every $d>0$.
There is a distance $d^{*}$ at which a daytime run and a night run would cost the same; solving $12+0.8d=12+0.8d+5$ finds it.
If the firm waived the $€\,12$ base on daytime runs only (charging pure $0.8d$), then for a $20$ km daytime job the client would save exactly $€\,12$ compared with the original daytime tariff.
If distance doubled from $10$ km to $20$ km on a daytime run, the bill would also double, because both the base and the kilometre charge scale linearly with $d$.
math.solution_overview: Day cost is the affine function $C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=12+0.8d$; night cost is the same plus a constant surcharge of $5$, so $C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)+5$. Their graphs are parallel (same slope $0.8$), so they never meet — the displayed break-even equation $12+0.8d=12+0.8d+5$ simplifies to the absurdity $0=5$. Waiving the $€\,12$ base on a $20$ km daytime job saves exactly $€\,12$ ($28\to 16$). Doubling distance from $10$ km to $20$ km multiplies the bill by $28/20=1.4$, not by $2$, because the intercept is fixed.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

By the stated tariff, every daytime job pays a fixed base of $12$ euros plus a proportional charge of $0.8$ euros per kilometre. For distance $d>0$ that is exactly the affine expression
$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=12+0.8d.
$$

Check a concrete sample: at $d=10$ one gets
$$
12+0.8\cdot 10=12+8=20,
$$
and at $d=25$ one gets
$$
12+0.8\cdot 25=12+20=32.
$$

No other fees are mentioned for daytime runs. The claim matches the tariff definition.

Writing the formula with euros made explicit: $C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=12+0.8d$ is the unique linear interpolant of the two tariff ingredients stated in the stem.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

By definition the night tariff is the daytime affine charge plus a flat surcharge of $€\,5$:
$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=12+0.8d+5=17+0.8d.
$$

Rewrite as a translate of the day bill:
$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)+5.
$$

Subtract the two bills:
$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)-C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=5
$$
for every $d>0$. The difference is a pure constant — it does not depend on distance at all.

Geometrically the night graph is a vertical translate of the day graph by five euros. The claim is true.

A concrete check at $d=10$: day bill $=20$, night bill $=25$, and $25-20=5$. At $d=100$: day $=92$, night $=97$, difference still exactly $5$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The displayed “break-even” equation is
$$
12+0.8d=12+0.8d+5.
$$

Cancel the identical affine parts $12+0.8d$ from both sides to obtain the absurdity
$$
0=5.
$$

There is no real $d^{*}$ satisfying it. Geometrically the two cost lines are parallel (same slope $0.8$) and vertically separated by $5$:
$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)-C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=5\neq 0
$$
for every $d$. They never intersect.

The algebra shown does **not** find a break-even distance; the claim is false.

If the night surcharge were distance-dependent the slopes would differ and a break-even could exist; here the surcharge is flat, so the lines stay parallel forever.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Compute the original daytime bill at $d=20$ kilometres:
$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)=12+0.8\cdot 20.
$$

First the kilometre charge:
$$
0.8\cdot 20=16,
$$
then add the base:
$$
12+16=28.
$$

If the firm waives the $€\,12$ base and charges the pure kilometre rate, the bill becomes
$$
0.8\cdot 20=16.
$$

The saving is
$$
28-16=12
$$
euros — exactly the waived base fee. The claim is true.

The saving equals the base fee for every $d>0$, not only at $20$ km: $C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)-0.8d=12$. The claim’s special case $d=20$ is representative.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Evaluate the daytime bill at the two distances:
$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)=12+0.8\cdot 10=12+8=20,
$$
$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)=12+0.8\cdot 20=12+16=28.
$$

Form the ratio:
$$
\frac{C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)}{C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)}=\frac{28}{20}=1.4\neq 2.
$$

Doubling distance multiplies the bill by $1.4$, not by $2$. The kilometre part scales ($8\to 16$), but the fixed base of $12$ does not; an affine function with nonzero intercept is not homogeneous of degree one.

The claim is false.

Homogeneity would require $C_{\mathrm{day}}(\lambda d)=\lambda C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)$ for all $\lambda>0$; plugging $\lambda=2$ and $d=10$ gives $28\neq 40=2\cdot 20$, a direct counter-example.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Letter-heavy polynomial limits and end behaviour
math.context:
Let
$$
p(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d,\qquad a\neq 0,
$$
be a real cubic, and define
$$
q(x)=\dfrac{p(x)}{x^{2}+1}.
$$
Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to+\infty}q(x)=+\infty$ whenever $a>0$.
$\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty}p(x)=-\infty$ whenever $a>0$.
If $p(1)=0$ and $p'(1)=0$, then $(x-1)^{2}$ divides $p(x)$, so $x=1$ is at least a double root.
For every choice of $a,b,c,d$ with $a\neq 0$, the horizontal line $y=0$ is a horizontal asymptote of $q$.
If $a=2$, $b=-3$, $c=0$, $d=0$, then $p(x)=x^{2}(2x-3)$, so $x=0$ is a double root and $x=\tfrac32$ is a simple root.
math.solution_overview: Divide the cubic by the quadratic denominator: $q(x)=ax+b+O(1/x)$ as $|x|\to\infty$, so end behaviour tracks the leading linear term $ax$. Whenever $a>0$ one has $q(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to+\infty$, while the cubic itself tends to $-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$. A common root of $p$ and $p'$ is a multiple root, so $p(1)=p'(1)=0$ forces $(x-1)^{2}\mid p(x)$. The line $y=0$ is never a horizontal asymptote when $a\neq 0$. The concrete coefficient choice $a=2,b=-3,c=d=0$ factors as $x^{2}(2x-3)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Perform polynomial division (or factor $x$ out of the leading terms):
$$
q(x)=\frac{ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d}{x^{2}+1}=ax+b+\frac{(c-a)x+(d-b)}{x^{2}+1}.
$$

As $x\to+\infty$ the rational remainder tends to $0$, because its numerator is linear while the denominator is quadratic:
$$
\left|\frac{(c-a)x+(d-b)}{x^{2}+1}\right|\le\frac{|c-a|\,|x|+|d-b|}{x^{2}}\to 0.
$$

Therefore
$$
q(x)\sim ax.
$$

Whenever $a>0$ one has $ax\to+\infty$, hence $q(x)\to+\infty$. The claim is true.

For a concrete illustration take $a=1$, $b=c=d=0$: then $q(x)=x^{3}/(x^{2}+1)\sim x\to+\infty$ as $x\to+\infty$, matching the claim.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A cubic is dominated by its leading term. Factor out $ax^{3}$:
$$
p(x)=ax^{3}\Bigl(1+\frac{b}{ax}+\frac{c}{ax^{2}}+\frac{d}{ax^{3}}\Bigr).
$$

As $x\to-\infty$ the parenthesis tends to $1$. With $a>0$ the leading factor behaves as
$$
ax^{3}\to-\infty,
$$
because the cubic power of a large negative number is negative and the positive coefficient $a$ preserves the sign.

Therefore
$$
\lim_{x\to-\infty}p(x)=-\infty.
$$

The claim is true.

The same leading-term argument with $a>0$ and $x\to+\infty$ would give $p(x)\to+\infty$; the odd degree is what flips the left-hand end behaviour to $-\infty$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

A standard root-multiplicity criterion: if a polynomial $p$ and its derivative $p'$ share a root $r$, then $(x-r)^{2}$ divides $p$.

Here $p(1)=0$ and $p'(1)=0$, so $r=1$ is a common root. Write the Taylor expansion about $1$:
$$
p(x)=p(1)+p'(1)(x-1)+\tfrac12 p''(\xi)(x-1)^{2}
$$
for some $\xi$ between $x$ and $1$. Both constant and linear coefficients vanish, so
$$
(x-1)^{2}\mid p(x),
$$
i.e. $x=1$ has multiplicity at least $2$. (For a cubic the multiplicity is then $2$ or $3$.) The claim is true.

Equivalently, write $p(x)=(x-1)^{2}(ax+\beta)$; the factor $(x-1)^{2}$ is forced by the twin conditions $p(1)=p'(1)=0$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

From the asymptotic expansion in A,
$$
q(x)\sim ax\qquad(a\neq 0),
$$
so as $x\to+\infty$ one has $q(x)\to\pm\infty$ according to the sign of $a$, and as $x\to-\infty$ the opposite infinity.

A horizontal asymptote $y=0$ would require
$$
\lim_{|x|\to\infty}q(x)=0,
$$
which fails whenever $a\neq 0$.

Concrete counter-example: take $a=1$, $b=c=d=0$. Then $q(x)=x^{3}/(x^{2}+1)\to+\infty$ as $x\to+\infty$, not to $0$.

The claim that $y=0$ is always a horizontal asymptote is false.

Degree counting also forbids a horizontal asymptote: numerator degree $3$ exceeds denominator degree $2$, so $q$ diverges at infinity whenever $a\neq 0$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Substitute the concrete coefficients $a=2$, $b=-3$, $c=0$, $d=0$:
$$
p(x)=2x^{3}-3x^{2}.
$$

Factor out the obvious common power of $x$:
$$
p(x)=x^{2}(2x-3).
$$

The squared factor $x^{2}$ shows that $x=0$ is a root of multiplicity exactly $2$. The remaining linear factor vanishes at
$$
2x-3=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad x=\frac{3}{2},
$$
and that root is simple because $2x-3$ appears only to the first power.

Check by differentiating: $p'(x)=6x^{2}-6x=6x(x-1)$, so $p'(0)=0$ (confirming multiplicity $\ge 2$ at $0$) while $p'(3/2)=6\cdot(3/2)\cdot(1/2)=9/2\neq 0$ (confirming simplicity at $3/2$). Both multiplicity claims hold.

The three roots of $p$ are therefore $0$ (double) and $3/2$ (simple), matching every clause of the claim.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Two entangled exponential–log functions — hard compare
math.context:
Define the entangled pair
$$
f(t)=5e^{0.25t},\qquad g(t)=20e^{-0.5t}\qquad(t\in\mathbb{R}),
$$
and the log-gap
$$
h(t)=\ln f(t)-\ln g(t)=\ln\!\bigl(f(t)/g(t)\bigr).
$$
Also write $p(t)=f(t)\,g(t)$. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $f(t)=g(t)$ has the unique real solution $t=\dfrac{4}{3}\ln 2=\dfrac{\ln 4}{0.75}$.
$h(t)=\ln 4+0.75t$ for every real $t$, so $h$ is affine with positive slope $0.75$.
If $t$ increases by $4$, then $f$ is multiplied by $e$ and $g$ is multiplied by $e^{-2}$.
The product $p(t)=f(t)g(t)$ is minimized over $\mathbb{R}$ at the same $t$ where $f=g$, and that minimum value equals $100$.
Because $f(0)=5<20=g(0)$ and $f$ grows while $g$ decays, one has $f(t)<g(t)$ for every $t>0$.
math.solution_overview: Equate $5e^{0.25t}=20e^{-0.5t}$ to get $e^{0.75t}=4$, so $t=(\ln 4)/0.75=(4/3)\ln 2$. The log-gap expands as $h(t)=\ln(5/20)+0.75t=-\ln 4+0.75t$, not $\ln 4+0.75t$. A time shift of $4$ multiplies $f$ by $e^{0.25\cdot 4}=e$ and $g$ by $e^{-0.5\cdot 4}=e^{-2}$. The product $p(t)=100e^{-0.25t}$ is strictly decreasing — it has no minimum at the crossing and is never constantly $100$. After the crossing $t^{*}>0$, the growing $f$ overtakes the decaying $g$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Set $f(t)=g(t)$:
$$
5e^{0.25t}=20e^{-0.5t}.
$$

Divide both sides by $5$ and multiply by $e^{0.5t}$:
$$
e^{0.25t+0.5t}=\frac{20}{5}=4\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad e^{0.75t}=4.
$$

Take the natural log:
$$
0.75t=\ln 4=2\ln 2.
$$

Solve for $t$:
$$
t=\frac{2\ln 2}{0.75}=\frac{2\ln 2}{3/4}=\frac{8\ln 2}{3}=\frac{4}{3}\ln 2=\frac{\ln 4}{0.75}.
$$

Because $t\mapsto e^{0.75t}$ is one-to-one on $\mathbb{R}$, the root is unique. The claim is true.

Numerically $t^{*}=(4/3)\ln 2\approx 0.924$, and $f(0.924)\approx g(0.924)\approx 6.32$, confirming a genuine crossing.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Expand the log-gap directly:
$$
h(t)=\ln(5e^{0.25t})-\ln(20e^{-0.5t}).
$$

Use $\ln(uv)=\ln u+\ln v$:
$$
h(t)=\ln 5+0.25t-\ln 20+0.5t.
$$

Combine constants and slopes:
$$
h(t)=\ln\!\Bigl(\frac{5}{20}\Bigr)+0.75t=\ln\!\Bigl(\frac{1}{4}\Bigr)+0.75t=-\ln 4+0.75t.
$$

The slope $0.75$ is correct, but the intercept is $-\ln 4=\ln(1/4)$, **not** $+\ln 4$. Numerically $-\ln 4\approx -1.386$ while $+\ln 4\approx +1.386$.

The displayed formula $h(t)=\ln 4+0.75t$ is wrong; the claim is false.

Evaluating the wrong formula at $t=0$ would give $h(0)=\ln 4>0$, but the true $h(0)=\ln(5/20)=\ln(1/4)<0$, already a contradiction.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Shift the time argument by four units and use the exponential addition formula:
$$
f(t+4)=5e^{0.25(t+4)}=5e^{0.25t+1}.
$$

Factor out $e^{1}=e$:
$$
f(t+4)=e\cdot\bigl(5e^{0.25t}\bigr)=e\,f(t).
$$

Likewise for $g$:
$$
g(t+4)=20e^{-0.5(t+4)}=20e^{-0.5t-2}=e^{-2}\bigl(20e^{-0.5t}\bigr)=e^{-2}\,g(t).
$$

The exponents come from the products
$$
0.25\cdot 4=1,\qquad -0.5\cdot 4=-2.
$$

Thus a time increase of $4$ multiplies $f$ by $e$ and multiplies $g$ by $e^{-2}$. The claim is true.

The growth factors are pure constants independent of $t$: $f(\cdot+4)/f(\cdot)=e$ and $g(\cdot+4)/g(\cdot)=e^{-2}$ hold identically.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Form the product explicitly:
$$
p(t)=f(t)g(t)=5\cdot 20\cdot e^{0.25t-0.5t}=100\,e^{-0.25t}.
$$

This is a strictly decreasing exponential in $t$. Its derivative is
$$
p'(t)=100\cdot(-0.25)e^{-0.25t}=-25e^{-0.25t}<0
$$
for every real $t$. It has **no** global minimizer on $\mathbb{R}$ (it tends to $0$ as $t\to+\infty$ and to $+\infty$ as $t\to-\infty$).

In particular it is not minimized at the crossing point $t^{*}=\frac{4}{3}\ln 2$, and
$$
p(t^{*})=100\,e^{-0.25t^{*}}\neq 100
$$
unless $t^{*}=0$, which it is not ($t^{*}\approx 0.924$).

Both halves of the claim fail; the statement is false.

At the crossing, $p(t^{*})=100e^{-0.25\cdot(4/3)\ln 2}=100\cdot 2^{-1/3}\approx 79.37$, which is strictly less than $100$ and is not a minimum.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

It is true that $f(0)=5<20=g(0)$ and that $f$ is increasing while $g$ is decreasing. But they meet at the positive time
$$
t^{*}=\frac{4}{3}\ln 2\approx 0.924>0
$$
from A.

For every $t>t^{*}$ the log-gap $h(t)=-\ln 4+0.75t$ is positive (because the slope $0.75>0$ and $h(t^{*})=0$), so
$$
f(t)>g(t)\qquad\text{for all }t>t^{*}.
$$

Concrete check at $t=2>t^{*}$:
$$
f(2)=5e^{0.5}\approx 8.24,\qquad g(2)=20e^{-1}\approx 7.36,
$$
and $8.24>7.36$.

The blanket claim that $f$ stays below $g$ for **every** $t>0$ is therefore false — it only holds on $(0,t^{*})$.

The crossing time $t^{*}>0$ is the precise threshold: $f<g$ on $(-\infty,t^{*})$ and $f>g$ on $(t^{*},+\infty)$.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Economic derivative of a tangled revenue path
math.context: A firm faces inverse demand $P(q)=120-4q$ for $0\le q\le 30$ (price in euros, quantity in thousands of units). Revenue is $R(q)=q\cdot P(q)$. Marginal revenue means $R'(q)$. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $R'(q)=120-8q$, so in particular $R'(5)=80$.
Revenue is maximised at the same quantity where $P(q)=0$, i.e. at the choke quantity $q=30$.
If output rises from $q=5$ to $q=6$, the linear approximation using $R'(5)$ overestimates the true revenue increase $R(6)-R(5)$, because $R$ is a concave quadratic.
At the quantity that maximises $R$, price equals marginal revenue.
Cutting price enough to raise quantity from $q=20$ to $q=21$ must raise revenue, because more units are sold.
math.solution_overview: Expand $R(q)=q(120-4q)=120q-4q^{2}$, so $R'(q)=120-8q$ and $R'(5)=120-40=80$. Revenue peaks where $R'=0$, i.e. at $q=15$ with $R(15)=900$, not at the choke $q=30$ where $R=0$. Concavity $R''=-8<0$ makes the tangent overestimate increments: the true rise $R(6)-R(5)=76$ is strictly less than $R'(5)\cdot 1=80$. At the peak, $MR=0$ while $P(15)=60$. Past the peak, $R(21)=756<800=R(20)$ despite selling one more unit.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Form the revenue function by multiplying quantity by inverse demand:
$$
R(q)=q\cdot P(q)=q(120-4q)=120q-4q^{2}.
$$

Differentiate term by term:
$$
R'(q)=120-8q.
$$

Evaluate at the concrete output $q=5$:
$$
R'(5)=120-8\cdot 5.
$$

Compute the product first:
$$
8\cdot 5=40,\qquad 120-40=80.
$$

Both the general formula for marginal revenue and the numerical evaluation match the claim. The statement is true.

As a quick consistency check, $R'(10)=120-80=40>0$ (still climbing) and $R'(20)=120-160=-40<0$ (already falling), bracketing the peak at $15$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Critical points of revenue solve $R'(q)=0$:
$$
120-8q=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 8q=120\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad q=\frac{120}{8}=15.
$$

At the choke quantity where price vanishes,
$$
P(30)=120-4\cdot 30=120-120=0,
$$
one has $R(30)=30\cdot 0=0$ as well — that is a boundary minimum of revenue on $[0,30]$, not the maximum.

The maximum value is
$$
R(15)=120\cdot 15-4\cdot 15^{2}=1800-4\cdot 225=1800-900=900.
$$

The claim equating the revenue peak with the choke quantity is false.

On the endpoints of the demand interval one also has $R(0)=0$ and $R(30)=0$, so the choke quantity is a second zero of revenue, never a maximizer.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The second derivative is
$$
R''(q)=-8<0,
$$
so $R$ is strictly concave. For a concave function the tangent line lies above the graph, and therefore overestimates finite increments.

Explicitly compute both revenue values:
$$
R(5)=120\cdot 5-4\cdot 25=600-100=500,
$$
$$
R(6)=120\cdot 6-4\cdot 36=720-144=576.
$$

The true increase is
$$
R(6)-R(5)=576-500=76,
$$
while the linear approximation is
$$
R'(5)\cdot 1=80.
$$

Since $76<80$, the tangent overestimates. The claim is true.

The overestimate gap is exactly $-\tfrac12 R''(\xi)\cdot 1^{2}$ for some $\xi\in(5,6)$ by Taylor’s theorem; with $R''=-8$ the gap is about $4$, matching $80-76=4$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

At the revenue-maximizing quantity $q=15$ one has
$$
R'(15)=120-8\cdot 15=120-120=0.
$$

The corresponding price is
$$
P(15)=120-4\cdot 15=120-60=60.
$$

Compare:
$$
P(15)=60\neq 0=R'(15).
$$

So price does **not** equal marginal revenue at the revenue peak. (The familiar identity $MR=P$ holds only for a price-taking firm; here the firm faces a downward-sloping demand, so $MR=P+qP'=P-4q$.)

The claim is false.

In fact $MR(q)=P(q)+qP'(q)= (120-4q)+q(-4)=120-8q$, which equals $P(q)$ only if $q=0$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Compute the two revenue values past the peak:
$$
R(20)=120\cdot 20-4\cdot 400=2400-1600=800,
$$
$$
R(21)=120\cdot 21-4\cdot 441=2520-1764=756.
$$

(Check the arithmetic: $4\cdot 441=1764$ and $2520-1764=756$.)

Quantity rises from $20$ to $21$ while revenue **falls** by
$$
800-756=44.
$$

Past $q=15$, the price cut needed to sell the extra unit destroys more revenue on infra-marginal units than it gains on the marginal unit. The claim is false.

Marginal revenue at $q=20$ is $R'(20)=-40<0$, so each extra unit past the peak reduces total revenue — matching the explicit drop from $800$ to $756$.

So the statement is False.

math.title: A Positive Test in a Deer Population
math.context: In a wild deer population, 60% are Subspecies A, 25% are Subspecies B, and 15% are Subspecies C. A certain prion disease is present in 2% of Subspecies A, 6% of Subspecies B, and 15% of Subspecies C. A field test for the disease has a 90% sensitivity (probability of a positive result if the deer truly has the disease) and a 4% false-positive rate (probability of a positive result if the deer does not have the disease), regardless of subspecies. A randomly tested deer receives a POSITIVE result.
statements: The probability that a tested deer receives a positive result is greater than 7%.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies A AND receives a positive result is greater than 3.4%.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies A, given a positive result is greater than 45%.
The probability that a tested deer receives a negative result equals 1 minus the probability that a tested deer receives a positive result.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies C, given a positive result is greater than the probability that the deer is Subspecies B, given a positive result.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The probability that a tested deer receives a positive result, $P(T^+)$, was calculated in the overview using the Law of Total Probability, considering the prevalence of each subspecies and their respective probabilities of a positive test:

$$
P(T^+) = 0.08257
$$

The claim states that this probability is greater than $7\% = 0.07$. We have:

$$
0.08257 > 0.07
$$

.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

This claim asks for the joint probability that the deer is Subspecies A AND receives a positive result, $P(S_A \cap T^+)$. This can be found using the conditional probability $P(T^+ \mid S_A)$ and the prior probability $P(S_A)$:

$$
P(S_A \cap T^+) = P(T^+ \mid S_A) P(S_A)
$$

From the overview, $P(T^+ \mid S_A) = 0.0572$ and $P(S_A) = 0.60$. Substituting these values:

$$
P(S_A \cap T^+) = (0.0572)(0.60)
$$

$$
P(S_A \cap T^+) = 0.03432
$$

The claim states that this probability is greater than $3.4\% = 0.034$. We have:

$$
0.03432 > 0.034
$$

.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

This claim asks for the posterior probability that the deer is Subspecies A, given a positive test result, $P(S_A \mid T^+)$. This requires Bayes' Theorem:

$$
P(S_A \mid T^+) = \frac{P(S_A \cap T^+)}{P(T^+)}
$$

From the calculations above, $P(S_A \cap T^+) = 0.03432$ and $P(T^+) = 0.08257$. Substituting these values:

$$
P(S_A \mid T^+) = \frac{0.03432}{0.08257}
$$

$$
P(S_A \mid T^+) \approx 0.415647
$$

$$
P(S_A \mid T^+) \approx 41.56\%
$$

The claim states that this probability is greater than $45\% = 0.45$. We have:

$$
0.415647 \not> 0.45
$$

.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

The events of a tested deer receiving a positive result ($T^+$) and a negative result ($T^-$) are complementary events. This means that if a test is not positive, it must be negative, and vice-versa. For any two complementary events, their probabilities sum to 1:

$$
P(T^-) = 1 - P(T^+)
$$

This is a fundamental property of probability for complementary events.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

This claim compares the posterior probabilities of Subspecies C and Subspecies B, given a positive test result: $P(S_C \mid T^+)$ versus $P(S_B \mid T^+)$. We calculate each using Bayes' Theorem.

For Subspecies C, given a positive test result:

$$
P(S_C \mid T^+) = \frac{P(S_C \cap T^+)}{P(T^+)}
$$

We need $P(S_C \cap T^+)$. From the overview:

$$
P(S_C \cap T^+) = P(T^+ \mid S_C)P(S_C) = (0.169)(0.15) = 0.02535
$$

Using $P(T^+) = 0.08257$:

$$
P(S_C \mid T^+) = \frac{0.02535}{0.08257}
$$

$$
P(S_C \mid T^+) \approx 0.3069
$$

For Subspecies B, given a positive test result:

$$
P(S_B \mid T^+) = \frac{P(S_B \cap T^+)}{P(T^+)}
$$

We need $P(S_B \cap T^+)$. From the overview:

$$
P(S_B \cap T^+) = P(T^+ \mid S_B)P(S_B) = (0.0916)(0.25) = 0.0229
$$

Using $P(T^+) = 0.08257$:

$$
P(S_B \mid T^+) = \frac{0.0229}{0.08257}
$$

$$
P(S_B \mid T^+) \approx 0.2773
$$

Comparing the two probabilities:

$$
P(S_C \mid T^+) \approx 0.3069 \quad \text{and} \quad P(S_B \mid T^+) \approx 0.2773
$$

.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
This problem describes a population of deer composed of three subspecies, each with a different prevalence of a certain prion disease. A field test for the disease has a known sensitivity and false-positive rate. We are testing a randomly selected deer and observing a positive result.

Let $S_A$, $S_B$, and $S_C$ be the events that a randomly selected deer belongs to Subspecies A, B, or C, respectively. Their prior probabilities are:
$$P(S_A) = 0.60$$
$$P(S_B) = 0.25$$
$$P(S_C) = 0.15$$

Let $D$ be the event that a deer has the prion disease. The prevalence rates for each subspecies are:
$$P(D \mid S_A) = 0.02$$
$$P(D \mid S_B) = 0.06$$
$$P(D \mid S_C) = 0.15$$

Let $T^+$ be the event of a positive test result and $T^-$ be the event of a negative test result. The test characteristics are:
Sensitivity: $P(T^+ \mid D) = 0.90$
False-positive rate: $P(T^+ \mid D^c) = 0.04$

This means:
$P(T^- \mid D) = 1 - P(T^+ \mid D) = 1 - 0.90 = 0.10$
$P(T^- \mid D^c) = 1 - P(T^+ \mid D^c) = 1 - 0.04 = 0.96$

To evaluate the probabilities involving test results, we first need to find the probability of a positive test result for a deer from each subspecies, considering its specific disease prevalence. This uses the Law of Total Probability for each subspecies:
$$P(T^+ \mid S_i) = P(T^+ \mid D, S_i) P(D \mid S_i) + P(T^+ \mid D^c, S_i) P(D^c \mid S_i)$$
Since the test characteristics are independent of subspecies, $P(T^+ \mid D, S_i) = P(T^+ \mid D)$ and $P(T^+ \mid D^c, S_i) = P(T^+ \mid D^c)$.
$$P(T^+ \mid S_i) = P(T^+ \mid D) P(D \mid S_i) + P(T^+ \mid D^c) (1 - P(D \mid S_i))$$

For Subspecies A:
$$P(T^+ \mid S_A) = (0.90)(0.02) + (0.04)(1 - 0.02)$$
$$P(T^+ \mid S_A) = (0.90)(0.02) + (0.04)(0.98)$$
$$
P(T^+ \mid S_A) = 0.018 + 0.0392 = 0.0572
$$

For Subspecies B:
$$P(T^+ \mid S_B) = (0.90)(0.06) + (0.04)(1 - 0.06)$$
$$P(T^+ \mid S_B) = (0.90)(0.06) + (0.04)(0.94)$$
$$
P(T^+ \mid S_B) = 0.054 + 0.0376 = 0.0916
$$

For Subspecies C:
$$P(T^+ \mid S_C) = (0.90)(0.15) + (0.04)(1 - 0.15)$$
$$P(T^+ \mid S_C) = (0.90)(0.15) + (0.04)(0.85)$$
$$
P(T^+ \mid S_C) = 0.135 + 0.034 = 0.169
$$

Now, to find the overall probability that a randomly tested deer receives a positive result, we use the Law of Total Probability over the subspecies:
$$P(T^+) = P(T^+ \mid S_A)P(S_A) + P(T^+ \mid S_B)P(S_B) + P(T^+ \mid S_C)P(S_C)$$
$$P(T^+) = (0.0572)(0.60) + (0.0916)(0.25) + (0.169)(0.15)$$
$$P(T^+) = 0.03432 + 0.0229 + 0.02535$$
$$P(T^+) = 0.08257$$
This is the base probability for many subsequent calculations.

math.title: Binomial courier audit — numbers only in the claims
math.context: A night courier logs 50 independent deliveries. Each delivery is on time with probability 0.8, independently of the others. Let X be the number of on-time deliveries among the 50. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: The expected number of on-time deliveries is 40, and the variance of that count is 8.
The probability of exactly 40 on-time deliveries equals the binomial probability with n = 50, k = 40, success probability 0.8.
The probability of exactly 41 on-time deliveries is strictly larger than the probability of exactly 40, because 40.8 lies closer to 41 than to 40.
If every delivery were certain to be on time, then the count would be 50 for sure and the variance would be 0.
After subtracting 40 and dividing by the square root of 8, the resulting number is exactly a draw from the standard normal distribution — not merely approximately.
math.solution_overview: The count $X$ is Binomial with $n=50$ and success chance $p=0.8$, so the mean is $np=50\cdot 0.8=40$ and the variance is $np(1-p)=50\cdot 0.8\cdot 0.2=8$. The probability mass at $40$ is exactly the binomial pmf $\binom{50}{40}(0.8)^{40}(0.2)^{10}$. The consecutive-odds ratio shows $\mathbb{P}(X=41)/\mathbb{P}(X=40)=(10/41)\cdot(0.8/0.2)=40/41<1$, so $40$ is the unique mode and the “$41$ wins because $40.8$ is closer” trap fails. Certainty ($p=1$) collapses variance to $0$. Centering and scaling yields mean $0$ and variance $1$ but keeps a discrete lattice law — it is not exactly standard normal.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The count $X$ follows a binomial law with parameters $n=50$ and success probability $p=0.8$. The expectation formula is
$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=np=50\cdot 0.8.
$$

Compute the product:
$$
50\cdot 0.8=40.
$$

The variance formula is
$$
\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)=50\cdot 0.8\cdot 0.2.
$$

First $0.8\cdot 0.2=0.16$, then
$$
50\cdot 0.16=8.
$$

Both numbers match the claim. Independence of the fifty deliveries is what licenses the binomial model and these closed forms.

As a Bernoulli-sum view: $X=I_1+\cdots+I_{50}$ with $\mathbb{E}[I_j]=0.8$ and $\mathrm{Var}(I_j)=0.8\cdot 0.2=0.16$, so $\mathbb{E}[X]=40$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=50\cdot 0.16=8$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

By definition, a binomial random variable with parameters $n=50$ and success probability $0.8$ assigns to the integer $k=40$ the probability mass
$$
\mathbb{P}(X=40)=\binom{50}{40}(0.8)^{40}(0.2)^{10}.
$$

That is precisely “the binomial probability with $n=50$, $k=40$, success probability $0.8$.”

Unfolding the binomial coefficient for transparency:
$$
\binom{50}{40}=\binom{50}{10}=\frac{50!}{10!\,40!},
$$
but the claim does not ask for a decimal evaluation — it only asks whether the probability equals that symbolic binomial expression, which it does by definition of the model stated in the stem.

The claim is true.

Nothing in the claim requires evaluating the decimal; equality of the probability with the binomial pmf at $(n,k,p)=(50,40,0.8)$ is the definition of the model.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A useful mode locator for a binomial count is $(n+1)p$. Here
$$
(n+1)p=51\cdot 0.8=40.8,
$$
which indeed lies closer to $41$ than to $40$ ($|40.8-41|=0.2<|40.8-40|=0.8$). But closeness of $(n+1)p$ to an integer does **not** decide which neighbouring mass is larger.

The exact consecutive-odds ratio is
$$
\frac{\mathbb{P}(X=k+1)}{\mathbb{P}(X=k)}=\frac{n-k}{k+1}\cdot\frac{p}{1-p}.
$$

At $k=40$:
$$
\frac{\mathbb{P}(X=41)}{\mathbb{P}(X=40)}=\frac{50-40}{41}\cdot\frac{0.8}{0.2}=\frac{10}{41}\cdot 4=\frac{40}{41}<1.
$$

Hence $\mathbb{P}(X=41)<\mathbb{P}(X=40)$. The unique mode is $40=\lfloor(n+1)p\rfloor$, not $41$. The claim is false.

The mode rule says: if $(n+1)p$ is not an integer, the unique mode is $\lfloor(n+1)p\rfloor=40$; the “closer integer” heuristic is simply the wrong rule.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

If every delivery were certain to be on time, the success probability would jump from $0.8$ to $p=1$. The binomial mean and variance formulas then give
$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=np=50\cdot 1=50,
$$
$$
\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)=50\cdot 1\cdot 0=0.
$$

A random variable with variance zero is almost surely constant, so
$$
\mathbb{P}(X=50)=1.
$$

Every delivery is on time for sure, and the count is $50$ with probability one. Both halves of the claim hold; the statement is true.

Equivalently, the pmf becomes a point mass $\delta_{50}$, whose second moment about $50$ vanishes, confirming variance $0$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The standardized variable
$$
Z=\frac{X-40}{\sqrt{8}}
$$
indeed has mean $0$ and variance $1$:
$$
\mathbb{E}[Z]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[X]-40}{\sqrt{8}}=0,\qquad\mathrm{Var}(Z)=\frac{\mathrm{Var}(X)}{8}=\frac{8}{8}=1.
$$

But $X$ remains a discrete random variable supported on the integers $\{0,1,\ldots,50\}$, so $Z$ is supported on a discrete lattice
$$
\Bigl\{\frac{k-40}{\sqrt{8}}:k=0,1,\ldots,50\Bigr\}.
$$

A standard normal random variable is continuous, with a density positive on all of $\mathbb{R}$. Therefore $Z$ is **not** exactly standard normal; the normal law is only a large-$n$ approximation (De Moivre–Laplace / CLT). The claim’s “exactly … not merely approximately” is false.

So the statement is False.
